--- format: revealjs: theme: ../../styles/meds-slides-styles.scss slide-number: true chalkboard: true title-slide: false jupyter: eds232-env --- ## {#title-slide data-menu-title="Title Slide" background="#053660"} [EDS 232]{.custom-title}
[Lesson 12]{.custom-subtitle} [*K-Means Clustering*]{.custom-subtitle} --- ## {#in-this-lesson data-menu-title="In this lesson"} [In this lesson]{.slide-title}

- Clustering as an unsupervised method for finding subgroups in data - The concept of a **centroid** and **within-cluster variation** - The **$K$-means algorithm** and how it minimizes within-cluster variation iteratively - Practical considerations: local optima, choosing $K$, and interpreting results --- ## {#section-example data-menu-title="# A guiding example #" background="#047C90"}

A guiding example

--- ## {#example-unlabeled data-menu-title="Elephant seal dive measurements"} [Investigating elephant seal diving strategies]{.slide-title}
Consider Amanda from our first lesson. She records **dive depth** (meters) and **dive duration** (minutes) for a large number of northern elephant seals — with no prior labels: ::: {.center-text .teal-text .body-text-m} *Are there distinct foraging strategies among these seals?* ::: ::: {#cell-unlabeled-data .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](12_k_means_clustering-SLIDES_files/figure-revealjs/unlabeled-data-output-1.png){#unlabeled-data width=1026 height=386 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: --- ## {#unsupervised data-menu-title="Clustering as unsupervised learning"} [Clustering as unsupervised learning]{.slide-title}
*Clustering* finds **subgroups** in a dataset so that observations within a cluster are similar to each other and different from observations in other clusters. . . . Unlike classification, there is no response variable $Y$ — no prior labels, no "correct answer." . . . Clustering is a type of **unsupervised** method: we discover structure within the data rather than predicting a known outcome. . . . ::: {.body-text-s} PCA is another unsupervised method we have studied: it finds a low-dimensional representation of the observations that explains a large fraction of the variance. ::: --- ## {#section-algorithm data-menu-title="# The algorithm #" background="#047C90"}

The algorithm

--- ## {#centroid-definition data-menu-title="What is a centroid?"} [What is a centroid?]{.slide-title}
A **centroid** is the average position of a set of points — the "center of mass" of the group. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="42%"} | Obs. | Depth $x_1$ | Duration $x_2$ | Cluster | |------|:---:|:---:|:---:| | 1 | 60 | 18 | A | | 2 | 210 | 6 | A | | 3 | 150 | 15 | A | | 4 | 240 | 26 | B | | 5 | 330 | 11 | B | | 6 | 360 | 29 | B | ::: ::: {.column width="58%"} . . . **Centroid of cluster A:** $$\bar{x}^{(A)} = \left(\frac{60 + 210 + 150}{3},\; \frac{18 + 6 + 15}{3}\right) = (140,\; 13)$$ . . . **Centroid of cluster B:** $$\bar{x}^{(B)} = \left(\frac{240 + 330 + 360}{3},\; \frac{26 + 11 + 29}{3}\right) = (310,\; 22)$$ ::: :::: --- ## {#centroid-plot data-menu-title="Centroid plot"} [What is a centroid?]{.slide-title}
::: {#cell-centroid-example .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](12_k_means_clustering-SLIDES_files/figure-revealjs/centroid-example-output-1.png){#centroid-example width=786 height=435 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: --- ## {#within-cluster-variation data-menu-title="Within-cluster variation"} [Within-cluster variation]{.slide-title}
For a good clustering, observations within each cluster should be as similar as possible. We measure this with **within-cluster variation**: $$W(C_k) = \frac{1}{|C_k|} \sum_{i,\, i' \in C_k} \;\sum_{j=1}^{p} (x_{ij} - x_{i'j})^2$$ ::: {.body-text-s} $|C_k|$ = number of observations in cluster $C_k$ — $p$ = number of features ::: ::: {#cell-within-cluster-variation .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](12_k_means_clustering-SLIDES_files/figure-revealjs/within-cluster-variation-output-1.png){#within-cluster-variation width=1025 height=384 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: --- ## {#objective data-menu-title="The K-means objective"} [The K-means objective]{.slide-title}

We want to find $K$ clusters that minimize the **total** within-cluster variation across all clusters: $$\underset{C_1, \ldots, C_K}{\text{minimize}} \left\{ \sum_{k=1}^{K} W(C_k) \right\}$$
. . . The $K$-means algorithm finds an approximate solution to this minimization through a simple iterative procedure. --- ## {#algorithm-steps data-menu-title="K-means algorithm steps"} [The K-means algorithm]{.slide-title}

1. **Initialize:** randomly select $K$ observations from the dataset as the initial centroids. . . . 2. **Assign:** assign each observation to the cluster whose centroid is nearest (smallest Euclidean distance). . . . 3. **Update centroids:** compute the new centroid (mean) of each cluster. . . . 4. **Repeat** steps 2–3 until assignments no longer change. . . .
::: {.body-text-s} Every iteration is guaranteed to decrease (or maintain) the total within-cluster variation, so the algorithm always converges. However, it does not always converge to the global minimum. ::: --- ## {#algorithm-iterations data-menu-title="K-means iterations"} [K-means in action]{.slide-title}
::: {#cell-algorithm-iterations .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](12_k_means_clustering-SLIDES_files/figure-revealjs/algorithm-iterations-output-1.png){#algorithm-iterations width=1350 height=825 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: --- ## {#section-considerations data-menu-title="# Considerations #" background="#047C90"}

Considerations

--- ## {#local-optima data-menu-title="Local optima"} [Local optima]{.slide-title}
Different random initializations can lead to **different final clusterings** — the algorithm finds a *local* minimum, not necessarily the global one. ::: {#cell-local-optima .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](12_k_means_clustering-SLIDES_files/figure-revealjs/local-optima-output-1.png){#local-optima width=1350 height=410 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.body-text-s .center-text} Run $K$-means many times with different initializations and keep the solution with the lowest WCSS. In `sklearn`: `n_init` parameter (default: 10). ::: --- ## {#choosing-k data-menu-title="How to choose K"} [How to choose $K$]{.slide-title}
$K$ is a hyperparameter chosen before running the algorithm. The **elbow method**: fit $K$-means for a range of $K$ values and plot WCSS vs. $K$. The *elbow* — where the rate of decrease flattens — suggests a reasonable value of $K$. ::: {#cell-elbow-method .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](12_k_means_clustering-SLIDES_files/figure-revealjs/elbow-method-output-1.png){#elbow-method width=706 height=385 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.body-text-s .center-text} Choosing $K$ also depends on what is practically meaningful or interpretable in the applied context. ::: --- ## {#interpreting-results data-menu-title="Interpreting results"} [Interpreting results]{.slide-title}
::: {.body-text-m} - Clusters will **always** be found — the algorithm partitions observations regardless of whether true subgroups exist. - Clustering with different parameter choices (different $K$, different initializations) will produce variable results. - **The output should not be taken as absolute truth**, but rather as a starting point for generating hypotheses and guiding further study. ::: . . .
::: {.body-text-m .teal-text} In Amanda's case, the clusters may correspond to real foraging strategies — but they could also reflect individual variation, seasonal patterns, or artifacts of data collection. ::: --- ## {#course-recap data-menu-title="Course recap"} [Everything we covered]{.slide-title}
